title: VT versus RR at the same minute ventilation
subtitle: Impact of shallow rapid breathing on dead space fraction and alveolar ventilation

patient.summary: A 45-year-old mechanically ventilated patient following abdominal surgery, sedated and fully adapted to volume control ventilation.

variable.label: Tidal volume & respiratory rate pattern (constant VE)

prediction.question: When tidal volume is halved and respiratory rate is doubled to keep total minute ventilation constant at 6.0 L/min, what happens to minute ventilation, PaCO2, and arterial pH?

whatToLookAtHint: Observe the total minute ventilation on the ventilator monitor alongside the arterial blood gas values for PaCO2 and pH.

reflection.question: Why does PaCO2 rise significantly despite total minute ventilation remaining unchanged at 6.0 L/min?

options.text: Fixed anatomic dead space is cleared on every single breath before fresh gas reaches alveoli; doubling the respiratory rate wastes dead space volume twice as frequently, reducing alveolar ventilation.
Halving tidal volume compresses pulmonary capillaries, directly impeding carbon dioxide diffusion across the blood-gas barrier.
A higher ventilator frequency triggers muscular shivering and doubles total metabolic carbon dioxide production.
Rapid cycling causes ventilator circuit gas compression, causing the ventilator to display a false minute ventilation reading.

reflection.explanation: Alveolar ventilation determines carbon dioxide elimination: VA = (VT - VD) × RR. Because anatomic dead space (150 mL) is constant for each breath, at VT 500 mL × RR 12, VA is (500 - 150) × 12 = 4.2 L/min. At VT 250 mL × RR 24, VA is (250 - 150) × 24 = 2.4 L/min. Alveolar ventilation drops by 43% despite identical minute ventilation (6.0 L/min), causing PaCO2 to accumulate and arterial pH to fall.

evidence.claim: Alveolar ventilation is the difference between tidal volume and dead space multiplied by respiratory rate, and determines arterial PaCO2.
evidence.source: West JB, Luks AM. West's Respiratory Physiology: The Essentials. 10th ed. Wolters Kluwer; 2016:15-28.

evidence.claim: Shallow rapid breathing increases dead space fraction (VD/VT) and causes hypercapnia despite preserved minute ventilation.
evidence.source: Nunn's Applied Respiratory Physiology. 8th ed. Elsevier; 2017:135-152.
